claim: Local translation can support memory consolidation by supplying new proteins to synapses undergoing plasticity.
source: Local translation can support memory consolidation by supplying new proteins to synapses undergoing plasticity.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific understanding about the role of local translation in memory.

claim: Translation in adult forebrain dendrites is an established mechanism of synaptic plasticity and is regulated by learning.
source: Translation in adult forebrain dendrites is an established mechanism of synaptic plasticity and is regulated by learning
evidence: This statement references established scientific consensus about dendritic translation.

claim: There is no evidence for learning-regulated protein synthesis in adult forebrain axons.
source: yet there is no evidence for learning-regulated protein synthesis in adult forebrain axons
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior evidence in the literature.

claim: Adult forebrain axons have traditionally been believed to be incapable of translation.
source: which have traditionally been believed to be incapable of translation
evidence: This statement refers to traditional scientific beliefs about axonal translation.

claim: Axons in the adult rat amygdala contain translation machinery.
source: Here, we show that axons in the adult rat amygdala contain translation machinery
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Over 1200 mRNAs in cortical axons projecting to the amygdala were regulated during consolidation of associative memory.
source: use translating ribosome affinity purification (TRAP) with RNASeq to identify mRNAs in cortical axons projecting to the amygdala, over 1200 of which were regulated during consolidation of associative memory
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the TRAP-RNASeq experimental data.

claim: Mitochondrial and translation-related genes were upregulated in axons after learning.
source: Mitochondrial and translation-related genes were upregulated
evidence: This finding is supported by the differential gene expression analysis and shown in Figure 4d and Table 1.

claim: Synaptic, cytoskeletal, and myelin-related genes were downregulated in axons after learning.
source: whereas synaptic, cytoskeletal, and myelin-related genes were downregulated
evidence: This finding is supported by the differential gene expression analysis and shown in Figure 4d and Table 1.

claim: The opposite effects on gene expression were observed in the cortex compared to axons after learning.
source: the opposite effects were observed in the cortex
evidence: This finding is supported by the differential gene expression analysis comparing axons and cortex, shown in Figure 4.

claim: Axonal translation occurs in the adult forebrain.
source: Our results demonstrate that axonal translation occurs in the adult forebrain
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the TRAP-RNASeq and immunoelectron microscopy data.

claim: Axonal translation is altered after learning.
source: and is altered after learning
evidence: This conclusion is based on the differential gene expression analysis comparing trained and control groups.

claim: Local translation is more a rule than an exception in neuronal processes.
source: supporting the likelihood that local translation is more a rule than an exception in neuronal processes
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.

claim: Memory consolidation requires new proteins to stabilize molecular changes induced by learning.
source: Memory consolidation requires new proteins to stabilize molecular changes induced by learning (Davis and Squire, 1984; Mayford et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Local translation in dendrites is thought to be an essential source of proteins for memory consolidation.
source: and local translation in dendrites is thought to be an essential source of these proteins (Sutton and Schuman, 2006)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Rich and diverse assortments of mRNAs have been described in neuropil of the mature hippocampus.
source: Rich and diverse assortments of mRNAs have been described in neuropil of the mature hippocampus (Poon et al., 2006; Zhong et al., 2006; Cajigas et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rich and diverse assortments of mRNAs have been described in cortical synaptoneurosomes.
source: and in cortical synaptoneurosomes (Ouwenga et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: No role for axonal translation in learning and memory has been reported in the adult forebrain.
source: Yet no role for axonal translation in learning and memory has been reported in the adult forebrain.
evidence: This statement describes the absence of prior evidence in the literature.

claim: Translation has long been known to occur in invertebrate axons.
source: Translation has long been known to occur in invertebrate axons
evidence: This statement refers to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Translation is essential for growth and response to guidance cues in developing CNS axons.
source: and it is now established to be essential for growth and response to guidance cues in developing CNS axons, and in regeneration of PNS axons (Akins et al., 2009; Twiss and Fainzilber, 2009; Jung et al., 2012; Batista and Hengst, 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Translation is essential for regeneration of PNS axons.
source: and it is now established to be essential for growth and response to guidance cues in developing CNS axons, and in regeneration of PNS axons (Akins et al., 2009; Twiss and Fainzilber, 2009; Jung et al., 2012; Batista and Hengst, 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Adult forebrain axons have been characterized as lacking the capacity for translation.
source: Adult forebrain axons, in contrast, traditionally have been characterized as lacking the capacity for translation, in part due to a lack of reliable evidence, and in part to the perception that they are structurally and functionally inert compared to dendrites and immature axons (Kindler et al., 2005; Jung et al., 2012; Batista and Hengst, 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research describing traditional views.

claim: Mature axons are capable of translation in some circumstances.
source: However, a number of recent studies have shown that mature axons are in fact capable of translation, at least in some circumstances (Willis et al., 2007; Gumy et al., 2011; Kalinski et al., 2015), including in the CNS (Taylor et al., 2009; Baleriola et al., 2014; Kar et al., 2014; Shigeoka et al., 2016; Hafner et al., 2019)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TRAP was used to isolate ribosome-bound mRNAs in retinal ganglion cells of adult mice.
source: but one study used translating ribosome affinity purification (TRAP) to isolate ribosome-bound mRNAs in retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) of adult mice (Shigeoka et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Ribosome-bound mRNAs are present in adult CNS axons in vivo.
source: demonstrating that ribosome-bound mRNAs are present in adult CNS axons in vivo
evidence: This statement is an inference from the cited study by Shigeoka et al., 2016.

claim: Presynaptic translation is necessary for long-term depression in hippocampal slice preparations from young animals.
source: Presynaptic translation has been shown to be necessary for long-term depression in hippocampal (Younts et al., 2016) and striatal (Yin et al., 2006) slice preparations from young animals
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Presynaptic translation is necessary for long-term depression in striatal slice preparations from young animals.
source: Presynaptic translation has been shown to be necessary for long-term depression in hippocampal (Younts et al., 2016) and striatal (Yin et al., 2006) slice preparations from young animals
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Axonal translation is involved in synaptic plasticity.
source: indicating that axonal translation is involved in synaptic plasticity and therefore could be important in memory as well
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies on presynaptic translation.

claim: Aversive auditory Pavlovian conditioning is supported by persistent strengthening of synaptic inputs to the lateral amygdala from auditory areas.
source: Aversive auditory Pavlovian conditioning (fear or threat conditioning), in which animals learn to associate an auditory tone with a foot shock, is supported by persistent strengthening of synaptic inputs to the lateral amygdala (LA) from auditory areas (Johansen et al., 2011)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The LA receives strong excitatory input from auditory cortical area TE3.
source: The LA receives strong excitatory input from auditory cortical area TE3 (Romanski and LeDoux, 1993; Shi and Cassell, 1997; Farb and Ledoux, 1999)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pavlovian conditioning induces persistent enhancement of presynaptic function at TE3-LA synapses.
source: and Pavlovian conditioning induces persistent enhancement of presynaptic function at these synapses (McKernan and Shinnick-Gallagher, 1997; Tsvetkov et al., 2002; Humeau et al., 2003; Schroeder and Shinnick-Gallagher, 2005)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Consolidation of memory requires translation in the LA.
source: Consolidation of memory requires translation in the LA (Schafe and LeDoux, 2000)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Memory consolidation induces changes in the translational machinery in LA dendrites associated with synapse enlargement.
source: and we have found that it induces changes in the translational machinery in LA dendrites associated with synapse enlargement (Ostroff et al., 2010)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Learning-induced structural changes occurred at individual axonal boutons as opposed to uniformly along axons.
source: Intriguingly, we also found that learning-induced structural changes occurred at individual axonal boutons as opposed to uniformly along axons, suggesting that plasticity may be as synapse-specific and compartmentalized on the presynaptic side as it is on the postsynaptic side (Ostroff et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Plasticity may be as synapse-specific and compartmentalized on the presynaptic side as it is on the postsynaptic side.
source: suggesting that plasticity may be as synapse-specific and compartmentalized on the presynaptic side as it is on the postsynaptic side (Ostroff et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the observation of synapse-specific structural changes.

claim: Early electron microscopy studies reported abundant polyribosomes in the somata and dendrites of neurons, but rarely in axons.
source: Early electron microscopy studies reported abundant polyribosomes in the somata and dendrites of neurons, but rarely in axons (reviewed by Giuditta et al., 2008 and Jung et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The paucity of conspicuous polyribosomes does not necessarily preclude translation.
source: However, the paucity of conspicuous polyribosomes does not necessarily preclude translation.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on subsequent evidence.

claim: Regenerating sciatic nerve axons contain mRNAs and translate membrane proteins in vivo, but do not show ultrastructural evidence of polyribosomes or rough endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Regenerating sciatic nerve axons contain mRNAs and translate membrane proteins in vivo, but do not show ultrastructural evidence of polyribosomes or rough endoplasmic reticulum (Zheng et al., 2001; Merianda and Twiss, 2013)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Hippocampal interneuron axons contain ribosomal proteins.
source: In addition, hippocampal interneuron axons contain ribosomal proteins (Younts et al., 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Translation sites other than classic morphological structures exist, such as periaxoplasmic ribosomal plaques found in adult spinal cord axons.
source: This suggests that translation sites other than the classic morphological structures do exist, such as the periaxoplasmic ribosomal plaques found in adult spinal cord axons (Koenig, 2009)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research and is an inference from the evidence.

claim: Translation can occur on 80S monosomes in yeast, with a bias toward highly regulated transcripts.
source: Recent work in yeast has shown that translation can occur on 80S monosomes, with a bias toward highly regulated transcripts (Heyer and Moore, 2016)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Polyribosomes have been occasionally observed in presynaptic boutons in the adult rat LA by EM.
source: We have occasionally observed polyribosomes in presynaptic boutons in the adult rat LA by EM (Figure 1a–b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–e), although these are infrequent (LO, unpublished observations)
evidence: This observation is supported by electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1.

claim: Polyribosomes in presynaptic boutons in the adult rat LA are infrequent.
source: although these are infrequent (LO, unpublished observations)
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the authors' unpublished data.

claim: LA axons may contain translation machinery that does not usually assemble into polyribosomal structures with traditionally recognizable morphology.
source: A possible explanation for this is that these axons contain translation machinery that does not usually assemble into polyribosomal structures with traditionally recognizable morphology, such as monosomes, whose morphology is not distinctive enough for unequivocal identification
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the infrequent observation of polyribosomes.

claim: Translation initiation is the most extensively regulated step in gene expression.
source: Because translation initiation is most extensively regulated step in gene expression
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific knowledge.

claim: Translation initiation is a critical mediator of memory formation.
source: as well as a critical mediator of memory formation (Santini et al., 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The eukaryotic initiation factors eIF4E, eIF4G, and eIF2α are present in axons forming synapses onto spiny dendrites in the caudal dorsolateral subdivision of the LA.
source: The eukaryotic initiation factors eIF4E, eIF4G, and eIF2α each were present in axons forming synapses onto spiny dendrites in the caudal dorsolateral subdivision of the LA (Figure 1c–e)
evidence: This finding is supported by immuno-electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ribosomal protein S6 is present in axons forming synapses onto spiny dendrites in the caudal dorsolateral subdivision of the LA.
source: as was ribosomal protein S6 (Figure 1f)
evidence: This finding is supported by immuno-electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The caudal dorsolateral subdivision of the LA receives the most robust projections from TE3.
source: which receives the most robust projections from TE3 (Romanski and LeDoux, 1993; Shi and Cassell, 1997; Farb and Ledoux, 1999)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Synapses with translation initiation factors have the same classic excitatory morphology as the glutamatergic projections from TE3 to LA.
source: These synapses have the same classic excitatory morphology as the glutamatergic projections from TE3 to LA (Farb and Ledoux, 1999), consistent with local translation on TE3 inputs
evidence: This is an inference based on morphological similarity and citation to prior research.

claim: 63% of axons in the LA neuropil contain eIF4E immunolabel.
source: Quantification of eIF4E immunolabel through serial sections of neuropil revealed that 63% of axons were labeled, along with 39% of dendritic spines and 100% of dendritic shafts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f–i)
evidence: This finding is supported by quantification of immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 39% of dendritic spines in the LA neuropil contain eIF4E immunolabel.
source: Quantification of eIF4E immunolabel through serial sections of neuropil revealed that 63% of axons were labeled, along with 39% of dendritic spines and 100% of dendritic shafts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f–i)
evidence: This finding is supported by quantification of immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 100% of dendritic shafts in the LA neuropil contain eIF4E immunolabel.
source: Quantification of eIF4E immunolabel through serial sections of neuropil revealed that 63% of axons were labeled, along with 39% of dendritic spines and 100% of dendritic shafts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f–i)
evidence: This finding is supported by quantification of immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Polyribosomes are found throughout dendritic shafts but in only a subset of dendritic spines.
source: Consistent with this pattern, we have previously found polyribosomes throughout dendritic shafts but in only a subset of dendritic spines, where their presence is regulated by learning (Ostroff et al., 2010)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: The presence of polyribosomes in dendritic spines is regulated by learning.
source: where their presence is regulated by learning (Ostroff et al., 2010)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: A viral vector was used to express an eYFP-ribosomal protein L10a fusion protein in TE3 cells in adult rats.
source: We used a viral vector to express an eYFP-ribosomal protein L10a fusion protein (Kratz et al., 2014) in TE3 cells in adult rats (Figure 2a–b)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, shown in Figure 2.

claim: Pilot experiments using an adeno-associated viral vector resulted in moderate to strong retrograde infection of cells in afferent areas.
source: Pilot experiments using an adeno-associated viral vector resulted in moderate to strong retrograde infection of cells in afferent areas
evidence: This is a description of pilot experimental results.

claim: A lentiviral vector did not result in retrograde infection.
source: To ensure that no cell bodies outside of the injection site expressed the construct, we switched to a lentiviral vector, which did not result in retrograde infection
evidence: This is a description of experimental results.

claim: Lentivirus has preferential tropism for excitatory neurons over inhibitory neurons in the cortex.
source: Lentivirus has also been shown to have preferential tropism for excitatory neurons over inhibitory neurons in the cortex (Nathanson et al., 2009)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: TE3 projections to the amygdala are excitatory.
source: which is advantageous since TE3 projections to the amygdala are excitatory
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the TE3-LA projection.

claim: Immuno-electron microscopy confirmed the presence of eYFP in LA axons.
source: Immuno-electron microscopy confirmed the presence of eYFP in LA axons (Figure 2c–f)
evidence: This finding is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2.

claim: TRAP was combined with Pavlovian conditioning to determine how the axonal translatome changes during memory consolidation.
source: TRAP was combined with Pavlovian conditioning to determine how the axonal translatome changes during memory consolidation (Figure 3a)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Animals expressing eYFP-L10a in TE3 were given either Pavlovian conditioning or exposure to the chamber alone.
source: Animals expressing eYFP-L10a in TE3 were given either Pavlovian conditioning, consisting of auditory tones paired with mild foot shocks in a familiar chamber (the trained group), or exposure to the chamber alone (the control group)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental groups.

claim: Unpaired tones and shocks were not presented to the control group because this paradigm constitutes a different type of associative learning and results in plasticity at LA synapses.
source: We did not present unpaired tones and shocks to the control group because this paradigm constitutes a different type of associative learning and results in plasticity at LA synapses (Rogan et al., 2005; Ostroff et al., 2010)
evidence: This is an explanation of the experimental design supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Long-term memory formation requires de novo translation during a critical period of several hours after training.
source: Long-term memory formation requires de novo translation during a critical period of several hours after training (Davis and Squire, 1984; Schafe and LeDoux, 2000)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Animals were sacrificed during the critical period for memory consolidation and separate tissue blocks containing either the auditory cortex or the amygdala were collected.
source: thus we sacrificed animals during this time window and collected separate tissue blocks containing either the auditory cortex or the amygdala (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The cortex samples contain the proximal axon segments, myelinated segments that pass through the dorsal portion of the external capsule, as well as intrinsic projections and corticocortical projections terminating in adjacent areas of TE1 and perirhinal cortex.
source: Although we refer to these samples as cortex and axons, the cortex samples also contain the proximal axon segments, myelinated segments that pass through the dorsal portion of the external capsule, as well as intrinsic projections and corticocortical projections terminating in adjacent areas of TE1 and perirhinal cortex (Romanski and LeDoux, 1993; Shi and Cassell, 1997)
evidence: This is a description of the tissue composition supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The term 'translatome' refers to the set of mRNAs that are bound to ribosomes.
source: We should also note that our use of the term 'translatome' refers simply to the set of mRNAs that are bound to ribosomes, and therefore past the initiation step of translation, but these transcripts are not necessarily undergoing active elongation or termination at the moment of capture
evidence: This is a clarification of terminology used in the study.

claim: Principal component analysis revealed correspondence between experimental replicates.
source: Principal component analysis revealed correspondence between experimental replicates, as well as separation between the TRAPed samples and the transcriptome, the cortex and axons, and the trained and control groups (Figure 3b)
evidence: This finding is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Principal component analysis revealed separation between the TRAPed samples and the transcriptome.
source: Principal component analysis revealed correspondence between experimental replicates, as well as separation between the TRAPed samples and the transcriptome, the cortex and axons, and the trained and control groups (Figure 3b)
evidence: This finding is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Principal component analysis revealed separation between the cortex and axons.
source: Principal component analysis revealed correspondence between experimental replicates, as well as separation between the TRAPed samples and the transcriptome, the cortex and axons, and the trained and control groups (Figure 3b)
evidence: This finding is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Principal component analysis revealed separation between the trained and control groups.
source: Principal component analysis revealed correspondence between experimental replicates, as well as separation between the TRAPed samples and the transcriptome, the cortex and axons, and the trained and control groups (Figure 3b)
evidence: This finding is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Gene expression levels were correlated between replicates.
source: Gene expression levels were correlated between replicates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: This finding is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Neuronal genes were more likely than non-neuronal genes to be enriched in the TRAPed samples versus the tissue transcriptome.
source: Comparison with a cell-type-specific proteome (Sharma et al., 2015) revealed that neuronal genes were more likely than non-neuronal genes to be enriched in the TRAPed samples versus the tissue transcriptome, whereas non-neuronal genes were more likely to be depleted (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c), confirming that our TRAPed samples contain mainly neuronal genes
evidence: This finding is supported by comparison with published proteome data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Non-neuronal genes were more likely to be depleted in the TRAPed samples versus the tissue transcriptome.
source: whereas non-neuronal genes were more likely to be depleted (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: This finding is supported by comparison with published proteome data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The TRAPed samples contain mainly neuronal genes.
source: confirming that our TRAPed samples contain mainly neuronal genes
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison with cell-type-specific proteome data.

claim: A conservative approach was taken to defining axonal genes in the dataset.
source: Because no translatome or transcriptome of adult forebrain axons has been previously published, we chose to take a conservative approach to defining axonal genes in our dataset (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a)
evidence: This is a description of the analytical approach shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Only genes that were differentially expressed between TRAPed samples were included to minimize false positives.
source: In order to minimize false positives introduced by the TRAP procedure, only genes that were differentially expressed between TRAPed samples were included
evidence: This is a description of the filtering strategy used in the analysis.

claim: Genes that were differentially expressed in the corresponding tissue transcriptomes were excluded.
source: Although this should account for much of the background from the experimental procedures, it does not account for differences between the background transcriptome of the tissue samples, and we therefore excluded genes that were differentially expressed in the corresponding tissue transcriptomes
evidence: This is a description of the filtering strategy used in the analysis.

claim: Genes that were differentially expressed between TRAPed samples were excluded if the enriched sample was not also enriched versus the tissue transcriptome.
source: Finally, genes that were differentially expressed between TRAPed samples were excluded if the enriched sample also was not enriched versus the tissue transcriptome
evidence: This is a description of the filtering strategy used in the analysis.

claim: The filtering method selected for more abundant genes with higher correlation between experimental replicates.
source: Examination of expression levels showed that our filtering method selected for more abundant genes with higher correlation between experimental replicates (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b)
evidence: This finding is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b.

claim: 1482 axonal genes were identified.
source: Of the 1482 axonal genes identified, the majority (1028) were also either regulated or enriched in the cortex (Figure 3c)
evidence: This is a summary of the differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The majority of axonal genes (1028) were also either regulated or enriched in the cortex.
source: Of the 1482 axonal genes identified, the majority (1028) were also either regulated or enriched in the cortex (Figure 3c)
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 3c.

claim: An additional 703 genes were regulated or enriched only in the cortex.
source: and an additional 703 genes were regulated or enriched only in the cortex (defined as 'cortex-only' genes)
evidence: This is a summary of the differential gene expression analysis.

claim: The actual population of axonal mRNAs is almost certainly larger than the stringently selected subset used for analysis.
source: It is important to note that although we are using the term 'translatome' to refer to the stringently selected subset of genes we used for analysis, the actual population of axonal mRNAs is almost certainly larger
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of the results.

claim: There was substantial overlap between genes enriched in the TRAP and eYFP-IP samples versus the tissue transcriptome.
source: As expected, there was substantial overlap between genes enriched in the TRAP and eYFP-IP samples versus the tissue transcriptome (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c)
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: There were very few learning-associated mRNAs in the eYFP-IP experiment.
source: There were, however, very few learning-associated mRNAs in the eYFP-IP experiment, and these had little overlap with the TRAPed mRNAs, and even less after the filtering step
evidence: This finding is from the eYFP-IP control experiment.

claim: There was only 2.5% overlap between axonal and cortical genes in the eYFP-IP experiment.
source: Although there was 47% overlap between axonal and cortical genes in the TRAP experiment (Figure 3c), there was only 2.5% overlap in the eYFP-IP experiment
evidence: This finding is from the eYFP-IP control experiment.

claim: The results of the TRAP experiment are not due to background.
source: These data confirm that the results of our TRAP experiment are not due to background
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the eYFP-IP control experiment.

claim: The most significantly enriched terms in axons related to mitochondria, translation, and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: The most significantly enriched terms in axons related to mitochondria, translation, and neurodegenerative diseases, whereas cortex-only genes were enriched for terms associated with the cell body, nucleus, and dendrites (Figure 3d)
evidence: This finding is from the DAVID analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Cortex-only genes were enriched for terms associated with the cell body, nucleus, and dendrites.
source: whereas cortex-only genes were enriched for terms associated with the cell body, nucleus, and dendrites (Figure 3d)
evidence: This finding is from the DAVID analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The filtering process did not dramatically skew the composition of the final dataset.
source: To ensure that our filtering process did not dramatically skew the composition of the final dataset, we also analyzed the unfiltered set of axonal genes. The resulting list of terms was similar, although enrichment levels were lower, consistent with a lower signal-to-noise ratio in the unfiltered data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a)
evidence: This finding is from the comparison of filtered and unfiltered data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3a.

claim: There was little similarity between the most enriched GO terms in the filtered data from the TRAP and eYFP-IP experiments.
source: Comparison between the filtered data from the TRAP and eYFP-IP experiments revealed little similarity between the most enriched GO terms (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b)
evidence: This finding is from the comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b.

claim: Terms relating to the presynaptic compartment and cytoskeleton were predominantly found in axons.
source: Manual grouping of significantly enriched terms revealed that terms relating to the presynaptic compartment and cytoskeleton were also predominantly found in axons, along with terms relating to various other cellular functions such as the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, GTPase signaling, and intracellular transport (Figure 3—figure supplement 4a)
evidence: This finding is from the manual grouping of GO terms shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4a.

claim: The size and composition of the TE3 axonal translatome are similar to what has been reported in other axonal and neuropil datasets.
source: The size and composition of the TE3 axonal translatome are similar to what has been reported in the translatomes of retinal ganglion cell axons (Shigeoka et al., 2016) and cortical synaptoneurosomes (Ouwenga et al., 2017), the transcriptome of adult hippocampal neuropil (Poon et al., 2006; Zhong et al., 2006; Cajigas et al., 2012), and the transcriptomes of axons isolated from cultures of dorsal root ganglion (Willis et al., 2007; Gumy et al., 2011), cultured motor neurons (Briese et al., 2016), and mixed cortical/hippocampal neurons (Taylor et al., 2009)
evidence: This is a comparison with published datasets supported by citations.

claim: 904 of the 1482 axonal genes (60%) were present in at least one published dataset.
source: We compared these datasets to our axonal and cortex-only translatomes and found greater overlap with the axonal genes, with 904 of the 1482 genes (60%) present in at least one published dataset (Figure 3—figure supplement 4b)
evidence: This finding is from the comparison with published datasets shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4b.

claim: At least some aspects of the axonal transcriptome are universal.
source: Given that these data were obtained from different cell types, preparations, ages, and species, this suggests that at least some aspects of the axonal transcriptome are universal
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overlap with published datasets.

claim: Transcripts associated with protein synthesis and energy metabolism are found throughout various axonal datasets.
source: In particular, transcripts associated with protein synthesis and energy metabolism are found throughout the various datasets
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison with published datasets.

claim: The axonal translatome had substantially more overlap with datasets from immature versus mature axons.
source: Interestingly, our axonal translatome had substantially more overlap with datasets from immature versus mature axons, potentially reflecting recapitulation of developmental mechanisms in learning
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison with published datasets, with a speculative interpretation.

claim: The majority of genes in the translatome (75%) showed differential expression following learning.
source: The majority of genes in the translatome (1647 of 2185 or 75%) showed differential expression following learning
evidence: This is a summary of the differential gene expression analysis.

claim: 40% of regulated genes showed significant changes in both axons and cortex.
source: Of regulated genes, 40% showed significant changes in both axons and cortex, and all but one of these (the mitochondrial enzyme Dlst) were regulated in opposite directions (Figure 4a)
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 4a.

claim: All but one gene regulated in both axons and cortex were regulated in opposite directions.
source: and all but one of these (the mitochondrial enzyme Dlst) were regulated in opposite directions (Figure 4a)
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The magnitude of change in the axons and cortex was significantly correlated for genes regulated in both areas.
source: The magnitude of change in the axons and cortex was significantly correlated for these genes, particularly for those downregulated in axons and upregulated in cortex (Figure 4b)
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Expression levels in the axons and cortex were significantly correlated in both training groups regardless of learning effects.
source: Expression levels in the axons and cortex were significantly correlated in both training groups regardless of learning effects, although genes that were upregulated in the axons showed the highest correlation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b)
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b.

claim: The axonal translatome is not regulated independently, but compartment-specific translation is coordinated within the cell.
source: These results suggest that the axonal translatome is not regulated independently, but that compartment-specific translation is coordinated within the cell
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between axonal and cortical gene expression.

claim: Only 63 genes encompassed the 50 most abundant in both areas and conditions.
source: This is underscored by the fact that only 63 genes encompassed the 50 most abundant in both areas and conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c)
